questions.solution_en:
Correct Answer: Option(A)

Explanation:

The "Both + Not" Rule: In formal English, the word "Both" is used only for positive (affirmative) statements. Using "Both" with a negative verb like "not" is a grammatical error.

The Replacement: To express a negative idea about two people or things, you must use "Neither."

Subject-Verb Agreement: The word "Neither" is grammatically singular. Therefore, it must be followed by the singular verb "has" instead of the plural "have."

Correct Sentence: Neither of the distinguished guests who were invited to the gala dinner has confirmed their attendance due to the sudden flight cancellations.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C).

Replace “that” with “what”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Conjunction "That" vs. Relative Pronoun "What" –

There is a significant difference between the conjunction "that" and the relative pronoun "what":

KEY POINT: “What” acts as conjunction + object of the verb.

In this sentence, the verb "saw" (at the end of the clause) is a transitive verb that requires an object—the witness saw something. If we use "that," the clause remains incomplete because "that" cannot act as the thing being seen. By using "what", we provide the object ("the thing which") that the witness saw.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1 : I know that you are a doctor. (Complete clause follows 'that') ✅

Example 2 : I know what you are hiding. ('What' is the object of 'hiding') ✅

Example 3 : She told me that she was hungry. (Complete information) ✅

Incorrect Usage -

Wrong example 1 : I cannot believe that he did to his best friend. ❌

Wrong example 2 : Do you understand that the teacher is explaining? ❌

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C)

Replace “very supreme” with “supreme”.

Rule / Concept: Absolute or Non-gradable Adjectives

Some adjectives express absolute or extreme qualities and cannot be intensified using words like very, more, or most.

Examples of such adjectives: impossible, universal, eternal, chief, ideal, supreme, perfect, unique, excellent, full, empty, entire, dead, free, circular, rectangular, etc.

Using modifiers like very or most with these adjectives is grammatically incorrect.

Corrected Sentence - After reviewing the governance framework and compliance protocols, the oversight committee concluded that the new guidelines were supreme in ensuring accountability.

More Examples for Clarity -

The design of the monument is unique. (Not “very unique”).

The solution proposed is perfect for the given requirements. (Not “more perfect”).

The circular auditorium is ideal for conducting large conferences. (Not “very ideal”).

Incorrect Usage –

The regulations are very supreme.

This approach is more impossible to implement.

questions.q_en:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

Despite limited resources and intense competition, the startup managed to __________ the ambitious project successfully.
questions.q_hi:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

Despite limited resources and intense competition, the startup managed to __________ the ambitious project successfully.
options_en: bring about
bring off
bring out
bring up
questions.solution_en:
Explanation: The correct answer is option (2).

English Explanation: “Bring off” means to succeed in doing something difficult or challenging. In the sentence, despite limited resources and intense competition, the startup successfully completed the ambitious project. Therefore, “bring off” correctly conveys the idea of achieving success in a tough situation. “Bring about” means to cause something to happen. “Bring out” means to reveal, publish, or highlight something. “Bring up” means to raise a topic or to nurture a child. Since the context refers to successfully accomplishing a difficult task, “bring off” is the most appropriate fit.

1. Bring about (उत्पन्न करना / कारण बनना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी घटना या परिवर्तन का कारण बनना।
Example: The reforms brought about significant changes in the system. (सुधारों ने प्रणाली में महत्वपूर्ण बदलाव उत्पन्न किए।)

2. Bring off (सफलतापूर्वक कर लेना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी कठिन कार्य को सफलतापूर्वक पूरा करना।
Example 1: It was a tough target, but the team brought it off through collective effort. (यह कठिन लक्ष्य था, लेकिन टीम ने सामूहिक प्रयास से इसे पूरा कर लिया।)
Example 2: She brought off a brilliant performance despite the pressure. (दबाव के बावजूद उसने शानदार प्रदर्शन किया।)

3. Bring out (प्रकट करना / प्रकाशित करना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी चीज़ को उजागर या प्रकाशित करना।
Example: The publisher brought out a new edition of the book. (प्रकाशक ने पुस्तक का नया संस्करण प्रकाशित किया।)

4. Bring up (उठाना / पालन-पोषण करना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी विषय को चर्चा में लाना या बच्चे का पालन-पोषण करना।
Example: He brought up an important issue during the meeting. (उसने बैठक में एक महत्वपूर्ण मुद्दा उठाया।)

questions.q_en: The proposal was neither practical nor financially viable, ______?
questions.q_hi: The proposal was neither practical nor financially viable, ______?
options_en: wasn’t it
did it
was it
didn’t it
options_hi: wasn’t it
did it
was it
didn’t it
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (c) - “was it”.

📌 Rule / Concept: “Neither…nor” = Negative Meaning + Auxiliary Repetition

The correlative conjunction “neither…nor” makes the sentence negative in meaning.

When the statement is negative → the question tag must be positive.

Also, when the main clause already contains an auxiliary verb (was/were/is/has etc.), we must repeat that auxiliary in the tag.

💢 Application to the Given Question

The proposal was neither practical nor financially viable

  • “Neither…nor” → negative meaning

  • Therefore → tag must be positive

  • Auxiliary used = was

  • Subject = “The proposal” → replaced by it

So, the correct tag is: was it?

✅ More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅- The report was neither accurate nor complete, was it?

Example 2 ✅- The policy is neither feasible nor affordable, is it?

Example 3 ✅ - The solution was neither efficient nor sustainable, was it?

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  • “Neither…nor” → treat as negative statement.

  • Negative meaning → positive tag.

  • Repeat the same auxiliary.

  • Do not be confused by two adjectives — focus on polarity.

questions.q_en: Select the sentence that is grammatically incorrect.
questions.q_hi: Select the sentence that is grammatically incorrect.
options_en: One-half of the employees were granted an early leave due to the festival.
Three-fourths of the office furniture was replaced during the renovation last month.
Two-thirds of the architectural plan have been drafted by the senior designer.
One-third of the milk has been used to prepare the dessert for the guests.

Three-fourths of the office furniture was replaced during the renovation last month.
Two-thirds of the architectural plan have been drafted by the senior designer.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (C)- The error lies in the verb agreement with the singular noun "plan."

Rule/Concept: Fraction & Proportion Agreement In sentences starting with a fraction or a word like "half," the verb does not look at the fraction. Instead, it "jumps" to the noun after the word "of".

If the noun is Plural: Use a Plural Verb.

If the noun is Singular or Uncountable: Use a Singular Verb.

Logic Breakdown:

(A) One-half of the employees were: This is Correct. The noun "employees" is plural, so the verb must be plural ("were"). This confirms that "One-half" takes a plural verb when the noun is plural.

(B) Three-fourths of the furniture was: This is Correct. "Furniture" is an uncountable noun. Uncountable nouns always take a singular verb ("was"), no matter how large the fraction is.

(C) Two-thirds of the architectural plan have: This is INCORRECT. The noun after "of" is "plan," which is singular. Therefore, the verb must be singular ("has").

(D) One-third of the milk has: This is Correct. "Milk" is uncountable, so the singular verb "has" is required.

questions.q_en: Select the sentence that is grammatically incorrect.
questions.q_hi: Select the sentence that is grammatically incorrect.
options_en: The poet and dramatist has been honored with the Sahitya Academy Award this year.
More than one student has successfully cleared the preliminary round of the exam.
Five miles are a long distance to cover on foot for an elderly person.
None of the information provided by the witness was found to be reliable.
options_hi: The poet and dramatist has been honored with the Sahitya Academy Award this year.
More than one student has successfully cleared the preliminary round of the exam.
Five miles are a long distance to cover on foot for an elderly person.
None of the information provided by the witness was found to be reliable.
questions.solution_en:
The answer it Option (C)- as it remains the incorrect sentence. The plural verb "are" should be replaced with the singular verb "is."

Rule 1 (The Primary Error): Units of Measurement When a plural noun (like miles, rupees, or liters) represents a specific distance, amount, or weight being treated as a single unit, the verb must be singular.

Incorrect: Five miles are a long distance...

Correct: Five miles is a long distance...

Why the other sentences are CORRECT (The Traps)

Why option (A) is correct: One Article Rule

"The poet and dramatist" uses only one article ("The") before the first noun.

This means one person is both a poet and a dramatist.

Therefore, the singular verb "has" is perfectly correct.



Why option (B) is correct: The "More than one" Rule

Although "More than one" sounds plural, it is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb.

"More than one student (singular) has (singular)..." is grammatically correct in formal English exams.

Why Option (C) is Correct: The "None of" + Uncountable Rule

In this sentence, "information" is an uncountable noun

When "None of" is followed by an uncountable noun, the verb must be singular.

Correct Sentence: Five miles is a long distance to cover on foot for an elderly person.

options_hi: The CEO was made resign after the internal inquiry.
The CEO was made to resign after the internal inquiry.
The CEO was made to be resigned after the internal inquiry.
The CEO resigned after being made by the board.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B)

📌 Rule / Concept: Causative Verb “Make” in Passive Voice

When “make” is used as a causative verb in active voice, it follows the structure:

Subject + made + object + base verb (without “to”)

However, in passive voice, the structure changes to:

Object + was/were + made + to + base verb

The word “to” becomes mandatory in passive constructions with “make.” This is a highly tested structural change in SSC and Banking exams.

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

In active voice, “make” takes bare infinitive (no “to”). In passive voice, “to” must be added. Never use “to be + V³” after “made” unless meaning genuinely demands it. This is a classic trap frequently tested in SSC CGL and Banking Mains examinations.

on minor market fluctuations during the volatile opening

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A)

Replace “such high-frequency trading algorithms fail” with “do such high-frequency trading algorithms fail”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Inversion with Negative Adverbs

Inversion is used with these adverbs (adverb of frequency):-

Seldom, Never, Hardly, Scarcely, Rarely, No sooner etc

When a sentence begins with a negative adverb or an adverb of frequency expressing a negative sense (such as Rarely, Seldom, Never, Hardly, Scarcely), the sentence must follow the Inversion structure. This means the auxiliary verb (do/does/did, has/have, is/are) must be placed before the subject, similar to the structure of a question, even though the sentence remains a statement.

💢 Application to the Given Question

Rarely such high-frequency trading algorithms fail...

In the sentence above, the adverb "Rarely" is placed at the beginning for emphasis. Therefore, the subject "such high-frequency trading algorithms" cannot be followed immediately by the main verb "fail". We must introduce the auxiliary verb "do" before the subject to satisfy the rule of partial inversion

corrected Sentence

Rarely do such high-frequency trading algorithms fail to capitalize on minor market fluctuations during the volatile opening hours of the National Stock Exchange’s morning session.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅: Seldom does he visit his hometown since he moved to London.

Example 2 ✅: Never have I witnessed such a lack of professional integrity in this office.

Example 3 ✅: Hardly had the meeting started when the power went out.

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  • Identify the Adverb: Always check if the sentence starts with a restrictive word like Rarely, Seldom, Never, or Hardly.

  • The Auxiliary Check: Ensure there is an auxiliary verb (do, does, did, has, have, had) between the adverb and the subject.

  • Tense Consistency: If the main verb is in the present tense (like fail), use do/does. If it is in the past tense, use did or had.

  • No Double Negatives: Do not use "not" in a clause that already begins with a negative adverb like Rarely or Seldom.

questions.q_en:
Select the passive form of the following sentence.

"The recovery agents laughed at the defaulter’s explanation."
questions.q_hi:
Select the passive form of the following sentence.

"The recovery agents laughed at the defaulter’s explanation."
options_en: The defaulter’s explanation was laughed by the recovery agents.
The defaulter’s explanation was being laughed at by the recovery agents.
The defaulter’s explanation was laughed at by the recovery agents.
The defaulter’s explanation had been laughed at.
options_hi: The defaulter’s explanation was laughed by the recovery agents.
The defaulter’s explanation was being laughed at by the recovery agents.
The defaulter’s explanation was laughed at by the recovery agents.
The defaulter’s explanation had been laughed at.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C)

📌 Rule / Concept: Simple Past (Phrasal / Prepositional Verb) – Active to Passive Conversion

In the Simple Past tense, the active structure is: Subject + V² + Object. The passive structure becomes: Object + was/were + V³ (+ by + Subject). When the verb is followed by a preposition (e.g., laugh at, look into, depend on), the preposition must be retained in the passive form. The tense must remain unchanged.

Usually, intransitive verbs (laugh) have no passive. However, if they are followed by a fixed preposition (laugh at), they become "transitive-equivalents."

The Reason: In the passive, the preposition "at" must stay with the verb, even if "by" follows it immediately. Option (A) is the trap for those who think "at" is redundant.

📌 Application to the Given Question-

The recovery agents laughed at the defaulter’s explanation. Here, “laughed at” is a prepositional verb in the simple past tense. “The defaulter’s explanation” is the object and becomes the subject in passive voice. Since it is singular, the correct auxiliary is “was.” The correct passive structure is: was + laughed at. Option (A) is incorrect because it omits the preposition “at.” Option (B) incorrectly changes the tense to past continuous. Option (D) shifts the tense to past perfect and omits the agent.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

Do not drop prepositions in prepositional verbs while converting to passive. Maintain the original tense. Use was/were + V³ for simple past passive. Check for subject–verb agreement carefully.

questions.solution_en:

The Rule: "Be used to" + Gerund (V1+ ing)-

When "used to" is preceded by a linking verb (such as is, am, are, was, were, get, or become), it functions as an adjective meaning "accustomed to" or "familiar with". In this specific structure, the word "to" acts as a preposition, not as part of an infinitive. According to the rules of grammar, a preposition must be followed by a Noun, Pronoun, or Gerund

The sentence describes the analysts' current state of being familiar with or habituated to a new way of working (video conferencing). Because "are" is present, the verb following "to" must be in the gerund form (conducting).

Why "conduct" is wrong: Using the base form ("conduct") would only be correct in the semi-modal structure "used to + V1” which describes a discontinued past habit (e.g., "They used to conduct briefings in person").

options_en: Before you leave to board an international flight, you
made sure that you have kept your passport and
boarding pass in an easily accessible pouch.
No Error
options_hi: Before you leave to board an international flight, you
made sure that you have kept your passport and
boarding pass in an easily accessible pouch.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “made” with “make”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Imperative Sentences and General Instructions

When a sentence provides instructions, advice, or a general rule for a future situation (often introduced by time conjunctions like before, after, when, or if), we use the Simple Present Tense (V1) to express the requirement. Using "made" in this context suggests that the traveler already performed the action, which contradicts the "Before you leave" instruction that addresses a future or general scenario.

💢 Application to the Given Question

"Before you leave... you made sure..."

In this sentence:

  1. leave is in the Simple Present, setting up a condition for a future action.

  2. made is in the Simple Past, referring to a completed action.

This creates a logical conflict. If you are currently giving someone a checklist for an international flight they are about to take, you must use the present form ("make") or a modal of necessity ("must make"). "Made" implies the check was done in the past, whereas the sentence is clearly providing instruction for an upcoming event.

Corrected Sentence

Before you leave to board an international flight, you make sure (or must make sure) that you have kept your passport and boarding pass in an easily accessible pouch.

questions.q_hi:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

He is one of our _______ who _______ always been ready to sacrifice their personal interests for the welfare of the organization.
options_en: employee / has
employees / has
employee / have
employees / have
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (D)

The blanks should be filled with "employees" and "have".

Rule 1: "One of our" + Plural Noun The phrase "one of our" implies a selection from a group. Therefore, the noun following it must be plural.

Correct: One of our employees.

Rule 2: Relative Pronoun (Who) Agreement When a relative pronoun (who, which, that) is used, the verb that follows it must agree with the antecedent (the noun immediately before "who"). In this structure, the antecedent is the plural noun "employees," not the singular "He" or "One".

Logic: ...employees (Plural Antecedent) + who + have (Plural Verb).

Correct Sentence: He is one of our employees who have always been ready...
